messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 32
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: City Council Member
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Vignette:
Priya was thirty-two when it happened, a warm September evening during her first term as a city council member. She had been standing near the stage at a community unity rally in a park she had never visited before—an unfamiliar neighborhood, a last-minute venue change. The explosion came from a trash bin twenty feet to her left. She remembered the sound as a pressure that pushed through her chest before her ears registered any noise, and then the screaming, the running, the bodies pressing against her from all directions. She had frozen for what felt like minutes, unable to move, until a police officer grabbed her arm and pulled her toward a gap in the fence. She ran, but she could not stop looking over her shoulder. In the weeks that followed, the city council held closed sessions about the attack—someone had planted a device, a man-made disaster born of political extremism. Priya attended every meeting, but she sat with her back to the wall, her eyes fixed on the door.

In the first months afterward, she began to notice small changes that she did not connect to the explosion. She stopped going to the gym because the feeling of her heart pounding during a run reminded her too much of that night; she had come to believe that any physical stress—sweating, breathlessness—made her vulnerable, as though her own body might betray her into helplessness. She started scanning every room before she could focus on a conversation. At council meetings, she would trace the exits with her gaze before sitting down, and if the only available seat was far from a door, she would stand instead, even as colleagues motioned for her to take a chair. She became vigilant toward people, especially men in crowds, watching their hands, their coats, the way they stood too still. What frightened her most was nightfall. She had come to feel that darkness collapsed the distance between herself and danger, that the world became something she could not see clearly enough to trust. She stopped attending evening events—town halls block parties, the annual lantern festival—and began leaving board meetings early, always before the parking lot emptied. Her staff noticed that she would circle the block twice before pulling into her own driveway, checking for anything out of place.

Her negative appraisals hardened into a fixed lens. She was certain that the world was fundamentally dangerous, that safety was an illusion she could no longer afford. She told herself that constant vigilance was not paranoia but prudence, that she had to be on guard all the time because you never knew what could happen next. She planned escape routes everywhere she went—the grocery store, the pharmacy, even her own living room during a friend’s dinner party. She avoided unfamiliar places altogether, insisting that council meetings be held only at the main municipal building, where she knew every corridor and stairwell. When a colleague suggested a community listening session at a new recreation center, Priya refused, saying the location was “not secure.” The colleague accused her of being inflexible; Priya did not explain that her heart rate spiked just thinking about walking into a room she had never seen. Over time, her refusal to attend night events or drive to unfamiliar neighborhoods cost her relationships with constituents and fellow council members. One senior colleague told her she was becoming “difficult to work with.” She knew he was right, but she could not make herself stop.

What finally brought Priya to seek help was the night she spent three hours parked in her own car outside a restaurant where a city council colleague’s retirement dinner was being held. She had driven there, sat in the lot, and could not make herself open the door. She watched other people walk in and out, laughing, not scanning, not calculating distances to exits. She felt her own isolation like a physical weight. She was afraid of losing her seat on the council, but she was more afraid that the world would never feel safe again. She wanted to believe that there was a way back—not to the person she had been before the explosion, but to a life that did not require constant surveillance of every shadow. She was not sure it was possible, but she called a therapist the next morning because she could no longer bear being the only one who was watching.
